passages.happening:
Paul has promised to show “the most excellent way” (12:31). Here it is.

“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal” (verse 1).

“If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing” (verse 2).

“If I give all I possess to the poor and exult in the surrender of my body, but have not love, I gain nothing” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is read at many weddings, and it is beautiful there. But Paul did not write it for a wedding. He wrote it to a quarrelling church: people split into parties over leaders, suing one another, eating while the poor went hungry at the Lord's Supper, and treating some gifts as marks of rank. It sits between two chapters about how they used their gifts in worship. It is a word to people who were hurting each other.

Every item in verses 1 to 3 is something the Corinthians prized. Tongues. Prophecy. Knowledge. Faith that does wonders. Great acts of giving. Paul names the best of them, and says that without love they are noise, nothing and no gain.

A gong and a cymbal were loud bronze instruments. They make a big sound and say nothing. That is what tongues without love are.

Paul says ‘I’, not ‘you’. He puts himself in the picture first. Even an apostle with every gift would be nothing without love.

Verse 3 has a small puzzle in the old copies. Two Greek words differ by one letter. Some copies read ‘so that I may boast’, and others ‘so that I may be burned’. The Berean Standard Bible follows the first, with ‘exult in the surrender of my body’. On either reading Paul imagines the greatest self-giving, done without love, and says it gains nothing.
passages.ot:
Love is at the heart of the Law. “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus named these two as the greatest commandments (Mark 12:30-31).

The prophets said the same about worship without love. “what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Gifts and sacrifices without love and justice did not please God.

‘Faith so as to move mountains’ echoes Jesus: “if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move” (Matthew 17:20).
passages.asks: Paul names the things his readers were proudest of and says they are nothing without love. Ask what you are proudest of in your faith: your knowledge, your service, your giving, your gifts. Then ask the people closest to you whether they would call you loving.

passages.happening:
Paul describes love by what it does and what it will not do.

“Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud” (verse 4).

“It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs” (verse 5).

“Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth” (verse 6).

“It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Read the list again with Corinth in mind. ‘Does not envy’: they were jealous of each other's leaders and gifts. ‘Is not proud’ is physioō, ‘puffed up’, the word Paul has used for them again and again (4:6, 18; 5:2; 8:1). ‘Not rude’ is the verb Paul used in 7:36 for ‘acting inappropriately’. ‘Not self-seeking’: each one went ahead with his own meal. Almost every line is the opposite of something the church was doing.

‘Patient’ is makrothymeō, literally ‘long-tempered’, slow to anger. It is the opposite of a short temper.

‘Keeps no account of wrongs’ uses a word for reckoning up, like a bookkeeper adding up a debt. Love does not keep a ledger of grudges, waiting to make the other pay.

Love ‘takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth’. Love is not soft on wrong. It cannot be glad when evil is done or covered up. It is glad when the truth comes out.

‘Bears all things’ can mean to cover or to put up with. ‘Believes all things’ and ‘hopes all things’ do not mean love believes every lie. They mean love does not give up on people; it keeps trusting God and hoping for good.

This is a portrait of Jesus as much as a rule. Put his name in place of ‘love’ and every line is true.
passages.ot:
The first words, ‘love is patient’, echo how God described himself to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Love that is slow to anger is God's own character.

Proverbs says, “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions” (Proverbs 10:12). That means love does not spread another's faults to hurt them. It never means hiding a crime or leaving someone in danger. The same book says, “Rescue those being led away to death” (Proverbs 24:11), and the prophets told God's people, “seek justice and correct the oppressor” (Isaiah 1:17).

God himself keeps no grudge against those he forgives: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).
passages.hard:
Does ‘love keeps no account of wrongs’ or ‘love bears all things’ mean that someone who is being hurt must stay silent, forgive and forget, and stay?

No. These notes say so plainly. Paul is describing love that does not hold grudges or seek revenge in ordinary life together. He is not telling anyone to hide abuse, to keep quiet about harm, or to stay where they are in danger. In the same breath he says love ‘takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth’ (verse 6). Covering up abuse is not love. Telling the truth about it is.

Keeping a record of what someone has done to you, for your safety or to get help or justice, is not a failure of love. It can be wise and necessary. Forgiving someone does not mean pretending it did not happen, or letting it happen again. Paul elsewhere says that the authorities are given to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and crimes should be reported to them.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And if anyone has used this chapter to tell you to stay silent, they have used love's own words against what love is.
passages.asks: Read verses 4 to 7 and put your own name in place of ‘love’. Notice where it stops being true. Ask God for help at that very point. Then put Jesus' name there, and notice that every line is true of him, and that he loves you this way.

passages.t: ‘When the perfect comes’: faith, hope and love
passages.happening:
“Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed” (verse 8).

“For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away” (verses 9-10).

“When I was a child, I talked like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I set aside childish ways” (verse 11).

“Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (verse 12).

“And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The Corinthians thought their gifts made them complete. Paul says every gift is partial. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge belong to the time before the end. Love belongs to both now and then.

Mirrors in Paul's day were polished metal, usually bronze. They gave a real image, but a dim and blurred one. Paul's Greek says we see ‘in a riddle’, ainigma. What we know of God now is true, but not yet clear.

‘Face to face’ is the language of seeing someone directly. ‘I shall know fully, even as I am fully known’ is the heart of it. God already knows us completely. One day we will know him as fully as we are able.

‘These three remain’. Faith trusts God. Hope waits for what he has promised. Love is the life of God himself shared with us. Paul says love is the greatest. One reason may be that when faith becomes sight and hope is fulfilled, love goes on.
passages.ot:
‘Face to face’ recalls Moses. “Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). God said of Moses, “I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8). Paul's word for the dim reflection is the word for a riddle, and he may have this verse in mind. What Moses had in part, all God's people will have.

A psalm longed for the same thing: “As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence” (Psalm 17:15).

And God's love is older than ours. “I have loved you with an everlasting love” (Jeremiah 31:3).
passages.hard:
What is ‘the perfect’ in verse 10? Christians read it in different ways, and the answer is tied to the question of whether gifts like prophecy and tongues continue today.

Some cessationists read ‘the perfect’, Greek to teleion, the complete thing, as the completed New Testament. On this view, once the Scriptures were complete, the partial gifts of prophecy and tongues ceased. Many cessationists, though, do not rest their case on this verse.

Most readers, and all continuationists, read ‘the perfect’ as what comes when Christ returns. They point to verse 12: ‘then we shall see face to face’ and ‘know fully’, which they take to describe the life to come, not this one. On this view the gifts continue until Christ comes.

Others read it as the church's maturity, or as the state of believers after death.

These notes do not choose. The site's notes on Acts 2 set out the views on gifts today. All agree with Paul's main point: every gift is partial, and love never fails.
passages.asks: Paul says we see dimly now. Ask where you need to hold your knowledge of God more humbly, and where you have treated a partial view as the whole. Then ask what it would mean to rest in this: whatever you do not yet know, you are already fully known.
